content: The geographical limitation of certain surveillance systems necessitates the implementation of broader surveillance strategies to ensure the detection of outbreaks. Among the pathogens included in invasive bacterial vaccine-preventable diseases (IB-VPD), only Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae are typically associated with outbreaks. While most pneumococcal diseases occur sporadically, outbreaks can arise in crowded environments such as military barracks, homeless shelters, and prisons. Similarly, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) can cause outbreaks in settings like daycare centers. Large-scale outbreaks of pneumococcal meningitis have also been documented in the African meningitis belt. There is no universally accepted definition for a pneumococcal cluster or outbreak. Some experts define a cluster as two or more temporally linked cases occurring in a closed setting. If the cases share the same serotype, the evidence for an epidemiological link is strengthened. In the African meningitis belt, a significant rise above baseline rates or crossing an epidemic threshold of 10 suspected meningitis cases per 100,000 population is often considered an outbreak. For invasive meningococcal disease (IMD), an outbreak is defined by the occurrence of a minimum number of cases of the same serogroup or strain within a defined time period or by exceeding a specific attack rate threshold, typically expressed as cases per 100,000 population. These thresholds vary by setting. A cluster refers to cases occurring close in time and within a defined geographical area or population, such as schools or prisons, but not meeting the criteria for an outbreak. A cluster may consist of two or three cases. A hyperendemic situation is characterized by persistently high levels of disease occurrence, often observed between epidemics in the African meningitis belt. In such cases, all patients must be treated promptly with appropriate antibiotics, and isolation protocols should be followed as per national guidelines. Pharyngeal swabs are not recommended, but specimens for laboratory confirmation should be collected before initiating antibiotic treatment whenever possible. However, treatment should not be delayed while awaiting laboratory results. In areas with a high prevalence of IMD, distinguishing IMD from other endemic hemorrhagic diseases, such as viral hemorrhagic fevers, is critical, and laboratory diagnosis plays a key role. For Haemophilus influenzae or Hib, there is no standard definition for an outbreak or cluster. Some experts consider two or more temporally linked cases in a closed setting as a cluster, with stronger evidence if the cases share the same serotype. Surveillance should be intensified during outbreaks and extended to all hospitals and clinics that may encounter meningitis, pneumonia, or sepsis cases. Active community-based surveillance and weekly reporting, including zero reporting, should be implemented to enhance case detection. Confirmed cases must be reported to the Ministry of Health on a monthly basis, and sentinel surveillance sites should adhere to zero reporting protocols. Aggregate reporting is sufficient for routine purposes, even if case-based surveillance is conducted. There are no global reporting requirements for pneumococcus under the International Health Regulations or WHO/UNICEF Joint Reporting Form. Each suspected case should be assigned a unique identification number. Core data elements for sentinel hospital surveillance of meningitis include site information, demographic data, clinical data, vaccination history, laboratory data, and dates of specimen collection and results. For population-based IPD surveillance, data should include the number of cases in the catchment area population stratified by age group. Data analysis for sentinel hospital IPD surveillance should include confirmed case counts stratified by onset date, age group, sex, and syndrome. Suspected meningitis, pneumonia, and sepsis cases should also be analyzed similarly. Mortality data, case fatality ratios, and vaccination status of cases should be included. Population-based IPD surveillance should calculate the incidence of confirmed cases stratified by similar parameters. Surveillance data should be used to determine the local disease burden, monitor epidemiological trends, prioritize IB-VPD among other public health concerns, advocate for control strategies such as immunization, and evaluate the impact and effectiveness of vaccination programs. Surveillance performance indicators, such as completeness of reporting, specimen collection rates, and laboratory confirmation with serotype determination, should meet specific targets to ensure robust data quality. Public health responses to IB-VPD cases should include hospitalization and prompt treatment with appropriate antibiotics, along with supportive care as needed. Specimens for laboratory confirmation should be collected before initiating antibiotics, but treatment should not be delayed. Countries should define specific actions for clusters or outbreaks, including further investigation, active case finding, and outbreak control measures. These measures may include case management structures, vaccination of at-risk populations, and antibiotic prophylaxis for contacts, tailored to the organism responsible for the outbreak. Reactive vaccination is a public health response to outbreaks caused by N. meningitidis but is not an established strategy for S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae. However, in large outbreaks of pneumococcal meningitis, particularly in Africa, reactive vaccination may be considered due to the high rate of sequelae. In Hib outbreaks, non-immunized or incompletely immunized contacts under 12 months of age should complete the vaccination schedule. Hib vaccination is generally not required for healthy children over five years of age. Chemoprophylaxis for meningococcal disease involves identifying close contacts and administering appropriate antibiotics, guided by national policies. Rifampicin is the preferred antibiotic, except for women on hormonal contraceptives (where ciprofloxacin is preferred) and pregnant women (where ceftriaxone is recommended). For Hib disease, chemoprophylaxis is recommended for at-risk household contacts, such as unvaccinated children under 10 years, partially vaccinated children under four years, and adults with asplenia or hyposplenism. It is not recommended for contacts of a single case in preschool settings but is advised if two or more cases occur within two months. Ciprofloxacin is the drug of choice, with ceftriaxone as an alternative. Chemoprophylaxis is not typically recommended for contacts of sporadic pneumococcal meningitis cases. However, in rare instances of pneumococcal disease clusters in settings like hospitals, long-term care facilities, prisons, military settings, hostels, or daycare centers, infection control measures, antibiotic prophylaxis, and vaccination of close contacts may be necessary. The choice of antibiotic should be guided by the in vitro susceptibility of the bacteria, the target population, and national guidelines.
